title: C# OOP versus JavaScript and TypeScript (runtime vs erased)
hook: TypeScript classes look like C# in a slide deck, but the Common Language Runtime (CLR) keeps types, access modifiers, and virtual dispatch slots at run time. The TypeScript compiler erases them — and interviews fail when you describe C# as just TypeScript with a runtime.

blocks.text: This topic compares how **object-oriented programming (OOP)** works in C# versus JavaScript and TypeScript. The core difference: C# types are **nominal** and exist as Common Language Runtime (CLR) metadata at run time. TypeScript types are **structural** and vanish when the compiler emits JavaScript. That single fact explains privacy, interfaces, virtual dispatch, value types, and why a Redis DTO that looked equal in JSON can still miss a Dictionary lookup in C#.

entries.plainDefinition: Types are equal only if they share a declared relationship (same class, implements interface). C# uses nominal typing.
entries.example: `AuthHint` and `CacheEntry` as separate classes are not interchangeable.

entries.plainDefinition: Types are compatible if their shapes match, regardless of name. TypeScript uses structural typing.
entries.example: `const hint: AuthHint = { key: "s" }; const entry: CacheEntry = hint;` — TypeScript allows this.

entries.plainDefinition: The process of removing type information during compilation. TypeScript erases types; C# preserves them in IL and CLR metadata.
entries.example: A TypeScript interface does not exist in the emitted .js file.

entries.plainDefinition: Runtime method routing through a method table. C# virtual/override uses this. JavaScript uses prototype chain lookup instead.
entries.example: `handler.Parse(raw)` calls the override on the runtime type.

blocks.text: If you ship both a .NET worker and a TypeScript client, you debug them differently. On the server, `private` is enforced by the CLR — ordinary Intermediate Language (IL) cannot read a private field from another type. On the client, TypeScript `private` is a compile-time error that disappears in the bundle. Auth tokens validated on the server are records with generated equality; the browser holds the same JSON as a plain object with no access modifiers and no `GetHashCode`.

blocks.title: The one-sentence summary
blocks.body: The TypeScript compiler strips types. The CLR loads them. That difference drives every answer on this page.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: Tracing a type from source to runtime

items.title: C#: compile to IL with metadata
items.body: Roslyn emits Intermediate Language (IL) that includes type names, access modifiers, virtual slots, and interface implementations. The CLR loads and enforces them.

items.title: TypeScript: compile to JavaScript without types
items.body: tsc removes interfaces, type aliases, and access modifiers. The output is plain JavaScript objects and functions.

items.title: C#: cast and is/as check at runtime
items.body: `if (handler is LtiHandler lti)` — the CLR inspects the object's actual type metadata.

items.title: TypeScript: type checks end at compile time
items.body: `if (handler instanceof LtiHandler)` works only for classes (runtime constructors), not for interfaces or type aliases.

diagram.title: C# metadata versus TypeScript erasure
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph csharp [C# path]
    CS[C# source] --> IL[IL plus metadata]
    IL --> CLR[CLR loads types]
    CLR --> RT[Runtime checks\ncasts, virtual, private]
  end
  subgraph ts [TypeScript path]
    TS[TS source] --> JS[JavaScript output]
    JS --> V8[V8 runs objects]
    V8 --> PROT[Prototype lookup\nno interface type]
  end

snippet.label: Structural typing that C# would reject
snippet.explanation: Line 1–2: two interfaces with identical shapes. Line 5: TypeScript allows the assignment because types are structural. Line 7: the emitted JavaScript has no type information — just a plain object assignment.

snippet.label: Nominal typing enforced by the CLR
snippet.explanation: Line 1 and 6: two classes with identical shapes but different names. Line 12: the compiler rejects the assignment — C# requires a declared relationship. Line 13: you must create a new instance or write a mapping. The CLR enforces this at compile time.

snippet.label: Virtual dispatch has no honest JS equivalent
snippet.explanation: Line 2: virtual opens a CLR dispatch slot. Line 7: override fills it. Line 11: calling through the base type dispatches to `LtiHandler`. In JavaScript, method lookup walks the prototype chain and can be changed at runtime — there is no fixed virtual table.

blocks.title: Calling TypeScript private the same as C# private
blocks.body: TypeScript `private` is a compile-time check — the emitted JavaScript has no access restriction. C# `private` is enforced by the CLR at runtime through metadata. They are not equivalent.

blocks.title: Assuming a TypeScript interface exists in a stack trace
blocks.body: When debugging a .NET exception, `is IAttemptStore` and interface names appear in stack traces. A TypeScript interface name never appears at runtime because it was erased during compilation.

interviewTakeaways: C# accessibility and interfaces survive as metadata; TypeScript types erase.
C# is nominally typed at runtime; TypeScript is structural at compile time.
Value types and virtual slots have no honest JavaScript equivalent.
commonPitfalls: Calling TypeScript private the same as C# private.
Assuming a TypeScript interface will exist in a stack trace.
